1. An evaluation of UNDP’s co-operation with Sri Lanka in the period 1998-2003 in the area of poverty reduction has to take into consideration the size of financial resources used ($ 18 million) compared with large financial resources of IFIs and bilateral co-operation. 

2.UNDP implemented various initiatives oriented to support Sri Lanka’s government and society in their objectives of reducing poverty. It has worked with the three sectors, State, private, and civil society. It has worked at different levels involving the national government, provincial, district and divisional authorities. There was also an emphasis to reach the poorest sectors by promoting CBOs to assume a catalytic role and emphasised downstream work with the hope of alleviating poverty and stimulate participation of peoples’ organisations and stakeholders. In recent years, UNDP has begun to work on soft assistance, including upstream advocacy and policy dialogue with the government, particularly in the context of the multilateral group.

2.The concept with which UNDP based its activities on poverty reduction could be considered sound. There was an attempt to follow a multidimensional approach that goes beyond income poverty to encompass access to markets, credit, social services, information and human rights.

3. UNDP gave priority to interventions oriented to ameliorate the effects of the armed conflict before and after the MOU by providing its developmental approach to rehabilitation, reconstruction, resettlement and reconciliation, in partnership with other UN agencies and bilateral donors. The work in the North and East is an important political sign that UNDP assumes its presence in the field as a UN agency in favour of peace and development.

4. With respect to the overall approach, UNDP interventions should consider the opportunity cost of interventions. While upstream activities may face political constraints and perhaps higher political risks, their payoff maybe much higher. The opportunity cost of downstream operations is quite high if outcomes benefit only a reduced number of persons, particularly if community development does not transcend the level of pilots to mainstream into development across sectors and themes. 

5. Considering upstream policies, UNDP did achieve contributions to outcome in terms of advocacy and beginnings of introduction of RBM at central ministries and provincial levels. Recent work related to human rights and governance, including parliament and access to justice are indicators that UNDP leadership gives priority to soft assistance and institutional change.

6. UNDP also contributed to the poverty debate in various ways (poverty conferences, civil society meetings, and dialogue with public officials, publication of a National Human Development Report in 1998).

7.Valuable documentation on experiences and policy proposals has been produced, which could have had strong influence on policy change. However, the fact that there was no emphasis on dissemination and follow-up to ensure public knowledge and use diminished the effect of the initiatives. For example, the documents were not all translated into the national languages.

8. In keeping with the thinking of the people and the government of Sri Lanka that devolution of power is strategic for peace and development, UNDP implemented a programme on an area-based strategy (ABGEP) in UVA province in close contact with the Provincial authorities. However, the lack of an enabling institutional arrangement for decentralisation hampered the outcomes of this initiative, in addition to specific design and implementation problems that are referred to below.  

9. Through projects, UNDP contributed to certain positive outcomes: sustainable activities and mobilisation of further parallel resources from donors (ABGEP); sustainable CBOs in the Programme of Catalytic Initiatives; generation of ideas, visions and planning practices in partner organisations, micro-credit network stepping into its sustainability.

10. In its downstream work, UNDP achieved progress in the outcome dimensions it established: “increased access of the poor to improved housing, finance, markets, technology and information”. The various projects supported installation of basic services, microcredit revolving funds, and provided technical support for income generating activities and access to markets and information. For example, fishing cooperatives in the North and East improved their access to markets in Colombo. Floriculture and vegetable producers in Uva Provinces were trained and gained access to the national market. The coverage is relatively small in terms of numbers of beneficiary population and families, insofar as the initiatives were mostly thought as pilots to be replicated.

11. Some obstacles that have hampered achievement of outputs and their contribution to outcome have been problems related to project design and implementation (quality of technical assistance, monitoring systems, procurement systems). The Transition Programme under DEX seems to show much higher cost-effectiveness than the former nationally-executed two initiatives (ABGEP and PCI).

12. In some cases, programmes have not reached sustainability because it was not duly incorporated in the planning stage (example: community radio in Uva Province, although there is now a planned effort to achieve sustainability).
